title: Email & IP security
syllabusUnit: Unit V: IP Security & Electronic Mail Security
covers: PGP, S/MIME, IPsec (AH, ESP, IKE), tunnel vs transport
learningGoals: You will be able to compare PGP's Web of Trust with S/MIME's hierarchical CA structure.
You will be able to distinguish IPsec Authentication Header (AH) from Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).
You will be able to contrast IPsec Transport mode and Tunnel mode.

lessonCards.title: Secure Email: PGP vs S/MIME
lessonCards.analogy: Sealing letters in wax stamped by friends (PGP Web of Trust) vs stamped by a notary public (S/MIME CA).
lessonCards.coreConcept: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) encrypts email using hybrid crypto and user-signed keyrings. S/MIME uses standard X.509 certificates issued by commercial CAs.
lessonCards.example: Both encrypt the email body and attachments, but leave email subject lines and metadata in the clear.

lessonCards.title: IPsec: AH vs ESP Protocols
lessonCards.analogy: AH puts a tamper-proof barcode on the envelope. ESP puts the letter inside a bulletproof armored briefcase.
lessonCards.coreConcept: IPsec operates at Network Layer 3. Authentication Header (AH) provides integrity and authentication (no encryption). Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality AND authentication.
lessonCards.example: ESP protocol 50 is the modern standard for VPN tunnels.

lessonCards.title: Transport Mode vs Tunnel Mode
lessonCards.analogy: Transport mode protects passenger mail; Tunnel mode drives the entire mail truck onto an armored bulletproof train.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Transport mode encrypts only the IP payload (data), leaving original IP headers visible (host-to-host). Tunnel mode encrypts the ENTIRE original IP packet and adds a new outer IP header (gateway-to-gateway).
lessonCards.example: Enterprise site-to-site VPNs connect branch offices using IPsec Tunnel mode.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between IPsec Transport Mode and IPsec Tunnel Mode?
options: Transport mode encrypts only the payload; Tunnel mode encrypts the entire original IP packet and adds a new outer header
Transport mode is for airplanes; Tunnel mode is for subways
Transport mode uses passwords; Tunnel mode uses biometrics
Tunnel mode cannot carry web traffic
questions.explanation: Transport mode protects end-to-end host communication; Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire IP packet inside a new IP wrapper for gateway-to-gateway VPNs.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Tunnel mode protects whole packets between VPN gateways.
Mode names refer to IP packet encapsulation architecture.
Both modes negotiate keys using IKE.
Tunnel mode carries all IP protocols (TCP, UDP, ICMP).
questions.realWorldExample: Corporate branch office routers use IPsec Tunnel mode to interconnect private subnets over the public internet.

questions.prompt: Between the two core IPsec protocols, Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), which provides CONFIDENTIALITY (encryption)?
options: ESP only (AH does not encrypt data)
AH only
Both AH and ESP encrypt data
Neither encrypts data
questions.explanation: AH (IP protocol 51) provides data integrity and anti-replay, but zero encryption. ESP (IP protocol 50) provides encryption, integrity, and authentication.
wrongExplanations: Correct! ESP provides confidentiality and optional integrity; AH provides integrity only.
AH never encrypts payload bytes.
AH cannot encrypt.
ESP encrypts payload data.
questions.realWorldExample: Because NAT routers modify IP header addresses, AH fails across NAT, making ESP with NAT-Traversal (NAT-T) the modern default.

questions.prompt: What protocol is used by IPsec to dynamically negotiate security associations (SAs) and exchange cryptographic keys?
options: Internet Key Exchange (IKE / IKEv2)
HTTP
FTP
Telnet
questions.explanation: IKE (running over UDP port 500/4500) uses Diffie-Hellman to authenticate endpoints and negotiate symmetric encryption and integrity keys.
wrongExplanations: Correct! IKEv2 negotiates encryption keys and security associations.
HTTP is an unencrypted application protocol.
FTP transfers files.
Telnet is unencrypted remote terminal access.
questions.realWorldExample: IKEv2 supports MOBIKE, allowing mobile phone VPN connections to switch between Wi-Fi and 5G cellular without dropping.

questions.prompt: How does Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) solve key authenticity without relying on centralized Certificate Authorities?
options: The Web of Trust: users cryptographically sign each other's public keys based on personal trust
PGP keys are published in local newspapers
PGP does not use public keys
By assigning keys based on social security numbers
questions.explanation: In PGP's decentralized Web of Trust, users verify identities in person (key signing parties) and sign public keys, creating a distributed web of endorsements.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The Web of Trust decentralizes identity verification without root CAs.
Newspapers are manual and non-cryptographic.
PGP is an asymmetric public-key system.
National IDs are not used in PGP keyrings.
questions.realWorldExample: Phil Zimmermann created PGP in 1991 to protect human rights activists and dissidents.

questions.prompt: Why do PGP and S/MIME still leak who you are emailing and what time you sent the message?
options: Email headers (From, To, Subject, Date) must remain unencrypted so mail servers (MTA) can route the message
Because encryption algorithms don't know how to encrypt text
Email protocols are illegal to encrypt completely
Because mail servers delete encrypted headers
questions.explanation: SMTP mail routers need cleartext To/From header fields to deliver email across the internet; only the email body payload is encrypted.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Email metadata remains unencrypted in transit.
Algorithms encrypt all binary data.
Full payload encryption is standard.
Servers forward headers, not delete them.
questions.realWorldExample: Metadata analysis (who talks to whom and when) can reveal sensitive relationships even when message bodies are encrypted.

questions.prompt: What email authentication framework uses DNS records to specify which mail servers are authorized to send email on behalf of a domain?
options: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) & DKIM
IPsec
PGP
Kerberos
questions.explanation: SPF DNS records define authorized sending IP addresses, while DKIM provides cryptographic digital signatures to block email spoofing.
wrongExplanations: Correct! SPF and DKIM combined with DMARC prevent domain spoofing and phishing.
IPsec protects network packets.
PGP encrypts message bodies.
Kerberos handles enterprise local SSO.
questions.realWorldExample: DMARC policies instruct receiving mailboxes (like Gmail) to quarantine or reject emails that fail SPF and DKIM checks.

ashRecap: IPsec shields raw network packets in armored tunnels. PGP and S/MIME lock your emails in digital envelopes so eavesdroppers can't read your mail!
